prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: Solar PV capacity additions by country and quarter, 2024 (MW) (language en).
Grid: 9 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes.
Merged cells: "Segment" spans 1 col × 3 row; "Europe" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Asia-Pacific" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Germany" spans 2 col × 1 row; "France" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Japan" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Australia" spans 2 col × 1 row.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Segment" · longest unbreakable unit 86px · widest one-line content 172px
  col 2: header "Europe › Germany › Q1" · longest unbreakable unit 40px · widest one-line content 40px
  col 3: header "Europe › Germany › Q2" · longest unbreakable unit 40px · widest one-line content 40px
  col 4: header "Europe › France › Q1" · longest unbreakable unit 33px · widest one-line content 33px
  col 5: header "Europe › France › Q2" · longest unbreakable unit 38px · widest one-line content 38px
  col 6: header "Asia-Pacific › Japan › Q1" · longest unbreakable unit 38px · widest one-line content 38px
  col 7: header "Asia-Pacific › Japan › Q2" · longest unbreakable unit 38px · widest one-line content 38px
  col 8: header "Asia-Pacific › Australia › Q1" · longest unbreakable unit 28px · widest one-line content 28px
  col 9: header "Asia-Pacific › Australia › Q2" · longest unbreakable unit 38px · widest one-line content 38px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 606px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). The table, including its 1px outer border, must be at most 606px wide (column widths sum to at most 605px); no horizontal scrolling. A table exactly 606px wide fits.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Your understanding: {"purpose":"Show solar PV capacity additions in MW across market segments, countries and the first two quarters of 2024.","tasks":["Look up a segment’s addition for a country and quarter.","Compare quarters within a country and corresponding quarters across countries.","Compare segment contributions with each country-quarter total."],"relations":["Europe groups Germany and France; Asia-Pacific groups Japan and Australia.","Each country has Q1 and Q2 columns, and each data row supplies values for all four countries.","The Total row aggregates the segments for each country-quarter."],"roles":["The first column identifies segments and the total; its header spans the three header tiers.","Regional and country headers group the quarterly columns beneath them.","Quarter headers identify the individual measures; numeric cells contain additions in MW."],"keep_whole":["Numbers, including thousands separators.","Quarter identifiers Q1 and Q2.","Country and region names, including Asia-Pacific.","Utility-scale and the other unbreakable units in segment labels."],"may_wrap":["Multiword segment labels may wrap at spaces, keeping their reading order natural."],"same_scale":["Quarter columns serve the same role and should have broadly comparable widths, while allowing for differences in numeric content.","Region and country headers derive their widths from their grouped columns.","The segment column needs a different scale from the numeric columns because its labels are longer."],"h_vs_v":"The viewport cannot accommodate every segment label on one line while preserving all numeric values. Giving the segment column more width can reduce wrapping; giving the quarterly columns more room produces a more open numeric grid at the cost of taller label rows."}

Image 1 is the one-line content overview. Then real browser renders of: d3r1A, d3r0A.
Measured facts:
d3r1A: column widths [136, 63, 63, 55, 60, 60, 60, 49, 59] px · table 606×361 px · row heights [36, 36, 36, 60, 60, 36, 60, 36] · column headers on >1 line: 0/15 · tallest cell 2 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · fits the 606 px viewport (no scrolling)
d3r0A: column widths [144, 61, 61, 54, 59, 59, 59, 49, 59] px · table 606×338 px · row heights [36, 36, 36, 60, 60, 36, 36, 36] · column headers on >1 line: 0/15 · tallest cell 2 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · fits the 606 px viewport (no scrolling)

Look at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design: what works, what is visually wrong, and the cause (which width). Then either propose up to 3 improved designs (refine the most promising, fix what you saw, or try an important unexplored idea) or, if further changes would not bring a meaningful improvement, set "done": true. Do not resubmit near-identical widths.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"best":["your best design name(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"change":"what and why"}]}
